Abstract How has the unprecedented salience of anti-Asian racism resulting from the CO­ VID-19 pandemic influenced Asian Americans’ coalitional attitudes, both withingroup and towards other racial minorities? Asian Americans, as the fastest-growing racial minority group in the United States, could play a key role in advancing racial justice. However, Asian Americans’ ambivalent racialization as valorized relative to Latino and Black Americans raises uncertainty as to how they will engage with other communities of color and racial politics. Using observational survey data from the 2016 and 2020 Collaborative Multiracial Post Election Study and an origi­ nal survey experiment, we find that COVID-19 era anti-Asian racism can begin to facilitate Asian American alignment with other communities of color, but it depends on how the issue is framed and only specific subsets of Asian Americans who are less socialized in racial discourses are persuaded by these frames. This study as­ sesses the challenges and possibilities of facilitating Asian American solidarity with other racial minorities.

Keywords  Coalitions · Solidarity · Discrimination · Asian American · Political views

## Introduction

The United States is projected to become a majority minority country by 2060. This expected trajectory has long been discussed, with the assumption that the country is at the precipice of political transformation. However, as others have warned, “demography is not destiny,” and a great deal remains unknown about the politi­ cal dynamics of a racially diversifying America, especially around the relationships between minority groups.

The political views and behaviors of Asian Americans in particular remain in ques­ tion as Asian Americans occupy an ambivalent position in the racial order. They are also the fastest growing minority group with a population that has almost doubled in the last two decades (Budiman and Ruiz 2021). Scholars of racialization have shown that while Asian Americans are civically ostracized relative to white Americans, they are valorized compared to Black and Latino1 Americans (Kim 1999; Masuoka and Junn 2013; Zou and Cheryan 2017) and benefit structurally from being “not-white, but above all not-Black” (Kim 2023). Considered the “racial bourgeoisie” (Matsuda 1996), Asian Americans are typically deemed by other racial groups as the least pro­ totypical group under the “people of color” umbrella (Pérez 2021). The ethnic diver­ sity of Asian Americans further complicates their group position since it is also a political question of when and where Asian Americans cohere pan-ethnically (Chan, Chong, and Raychaudhuri 2021; Espiritu 1992; Okamoto 2014; Wu 2022). In short, Asian Americans are distinct from other racial minorities across a variety of markers.

The question of how Asian Americans fit in racial politics has been put to test by the rise in anti-Asian racism during the COVID-19 pandemic (Chan and Leung 2024; Hua and Junn 2021). While anti-Asian racism has always been deeply embedded in the history of the United States (Man 2020), this wave of anti-Asian racism has served as a potent reminder to Asian Americans of their precarious place in American society. It has motivated a level of racial consciousness and mobilization amongst Asian communities unseen in recent memory. The Stop Asian Hate movement also comes on the heels of another Asian American reckoning: one spurred by the Move­ ment for Black Lives, where Asian Americans were faced with their relative privilege and complicity in maintaining the status quo as a non-Black racial minority. These contemporaneous movements have marked a pivotal moment for Asian American politics, urging them to define and articulate their place in the country’s racial politics.

In this paper, we ask: what are the impacts of anti-Asian racism during the COVID- 19 pandemic on Asian American solidarity? Through the case of Asian Americans, we investigate the conditions under which perceiving discrimination against your own group increases feelings of solidarity within the group as well as with other minoritized groups. We examine these questions through analyses of nationally rep­ resentative survey data from 2016 to 2020 and an original survey experiment. While the work of building solidarity requires sustained and deep commitment, a kind of engagement that cannot be fully induced nor captured by a survey experiment (Chen and Hosam 2022; Fu et al. 2019; Wong 2021), our study seeks to identify whether

Asian Americans connect their own marginalization with that of other groups and, in doing so, take the first steps towards engaging in coalition.

The issue of racialized violence is one that affects communities of color across the board, even if the nature and scale of such violence may be incommensurate between groups (Kim 2023; Sexton 2010). While the issue of anti-Asian hate received a lot of attention during the COVID-19 years, data from the Federal Bureau of Investiga­ tion showed that in 2020, over half of reported race-based hate crimes were against Black Americans, 10% were against Latinos, and 5% were against Asian Americans (Wong and Liu 2022).2 This illustrates that the issue of anti-Asian hate incidents is part of a broader pattern of violence against minoritized groups. We thus believe it is important that Asian Americans, in light of COVID-19 anti-Asian racism, also become more aware of the racial injustices facing other groups and more supportive of the efforts to address them.

We find that COVID-19 era anti-Asian racism can begin to facilitate Asian Ameri­ can feelings of solidarity with other communities of color, but how narratives about discrimination are framed and to whom those messages are conveyed matter. In particular, information about anti-Asian racism positively shifted Republican Asian Americans and first-generation Asian Americans’ attitudes towards Black and Latino Americans. Additionally, when anti-Asian racism is framed as being connected to discrimination against other racial minority groups, the information increased Repub­ lican Asian Americans’ support for policies and movements that focus on Black and Latino communities.

Despite these encouraging results, treatment effects from our survey experiments are mixed. As such, our treatment effects, when examined in context with respon­ dents’ open text responses, offer further insight into the difficult and contingent nature of building Asian American solidarity. We argue that the challenges of mobilizing Asian Americans to work in coalition with other racial minorities, even in light of unprecedented salience of anti-Asian racism, stem from the political and social con­ struction of Asian Americans as a racial minority group that is valorized relative to others. With these results, our paper contributes to understanding Asian Americans’ reactions to their political socialization, as well as recognizing heterogeneity within Asian Americans.

Theory & Hypotheses

Key political psychology theories provide differing answers for whether we would expect Asian Americans to express more closeness with other racial minorities amidst the rise of anti-Asian racism. Scholarship on social identity threat has shown that per­ ceiving threat against one’s identity can strengthen positive feelings towards the ingroup and lead to the derogation of out-groups, including other marginalized groups (Branscombe et al. 1999; Craig et al. 2012). This suggests that perceiving more anti-Asian racism may increase Asian American solidarity within-group, and not only discourage a sense of similarity with other racial minorities, but even lead to the derogation of other groups.

Meanwhile, another strand of political psychology has argued that perceived discrimination against one’s own group can help facilitate commonality with other marginalized groups. Experimental studies have shown that generating a common ingroup identity of being racially marginalized (Craig and Richeson 2012) or high­ lighting shared experiences of discrimination (Cortland et al. 2017) can increase positive feeling towards and perceived similarity with other minoritized groups. This is reflected in the increasing popularity of umbrella identities like people-of-color (POC) identity. Pérez (2021) illustrates how a term like POC can cut across exist­ ing racial identities, while still co-existing with them, and produce a shared identity amongst those who might have been previously thought of as different groups. Thus, while the increased visibility of anti-Asian racism may fuel social identity threat, it may also be an opening to facilitate coalitional attitudes.

Material or status concerns can also hinder the formation of racial solidarity. Groups are especially vulnerable to conflict when the resources in question are scarce or zero-sum (Blalock 1967; Browning, Marshall, and Tabb 2002; McClain and Tau­ ber 2001). Racially minoritized groups may also compete over status in the racial order (Blumer 1958; Masuoka and Junn 2013; Kim 1999; Pérez et al. 2022; Zou and Cheryan 2017). Pérez, Robertson, and Vicuña (2022) find that groups who are located “along an in-group’s periphery,” Latinos in their case, can be motivated to express anti-Black racism to protect their own sense of belonging when they feel that is being threatened. Threat can motivate marginalized groups to defend and justify the status quo, as is argued in System Justification Theory (SJT) (Jost, Banaji, and Nosek 2004). Conversely, emphasizing a shared source of marginalization, such as Latinos and Asian Americans both being racialized as foreign, can help build com­ monality between groups (Pérez et al. 2022).

Much of the literature on intergroup dynamics has focused on Black-Latino rela­ tions and this study builds upon the rich insights from these works (Benjamin 2017; Kaufmann 2003; Krupnikov and Piston 2016; McClain 1993; Pérez, Robertson, and Vicuña 2022; Wilkinson 2015). However, theories of racial positioning suggest that we should have different empirical expectations for how Asian Americans engage with other minority groups as they are triangulated in the racial order: racialized as perpetual foreigners but valorized relative to Black Americans (Kim 1999). More recently, Kim (2023) has shown that central to the racialization of Asian Americans is serving as the foil to Black Americans. Scholars have extended Kim’s (1999) work through the lens of immigration policy (Masuoka and Junn 2013) and social psychol­ ogy (Zou and Cheryan 2017) to show that Asian Americans are also valorized relative to Latino communities. The fraught place of Asian Americans in the American racial order makes the group a pivotal yet uncertain actor in racial politics (Kim 2004; Kim and Lee 2001 ). What does it mean for Asian American engagement in people of color politics if Asian Americans are racialized as of higher status and thus differenti­ ated from other racial minorities?

Asian Americans offer a hard test for the challenges and possibilities of allyship between racial minorities. The group’s political behavior reflects their ambivalent position within the racial order. Electorally, Asian Americans are increasingly voting Democrat (Raychaudhuri 2018) and were part of the unprecedented turnout among voters of color to elect Barack Obama twice (Ramakrishnan 2014). Many of their policy attitudes align more with African Americans’ and Latinos’ policy attitudes compared to white Americans’ policy attitudes (Arora, Sadhwani, and Shah 2021; Ramakrishnan 2014). At the same time, recent years have also seen a highly influen­ tial conservative segment of the community, mainly Chinese Americans, challenge race-conscious admissions policies (Poon et al. 2019). These anti-affirmative action activists often demarcate Asian American interests from those of other communi­ ties of color, claiming that Black and Latino students benefit from affirmative action at the expense of Asian American students (Kim 2018; Poon et al. 2019). Whether Asian Americans see themselves as aligned with other communities of color has sig­ nificant consequences for policies and movements for racial justice like affirmative action (Liu and Carrington 2022), a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immi­ grants (Samson 2015), and the Black Lives Matter movement (Merseth 2018).

Despite the role of material or status concerns in fueling intergroup conflict, we have reason to think that this wave of anti-Asian racism may facilitate coalitional pol­ itics with other minoritized groups. Prior to the pandemic, perceived discrimination by Asian Americans was associated with feelings of commonality with Black and Latino Americans (Huang 2021). The rise of anti-Asian racism in 2020 then made clear how Asian Americans’ racialization as high-status (Zou and Cheryan 2017) was always co-constitutive with their racialization as foreign, disease-ridden, and disloyal (Tessler, Choi, and Kao 2020). Anti-Asian racism received an unprecedented level of attention during the pandemic, creating an information environment that funda­ mentally altered daily life for many Asian Americans. Particularly for those who are relatively privileged by being light-skinned or being of higher socio-economic status, contemporary anti-Asian racism has been a significant reminder for Asian Americans of their precarious place in American society.

There is some evidence that anti-Asian racism from the COVID-19 era has impacted Asian American political identity, specifically in terms of partisan identifi­ cation. Asian Americans were more likely to view the Democratic party more favor­ ably after Donald Trump’s use of anti-Asian rhetoric in early 2020 (Chan, Kim, and Leung 2021). In the 2020 election, Asian Americans with stronger perceptions of racial discrimination were more likely to vote for the Democratic party (Chan, Nguy, and Masuoka 2022). These findings align with previous accounts that argue Asian Americans tend to have weaker identification with the two-party system (Hajnal and Lee 2011; Wong et al. 2011), making their partisan allegiances more open to dynamics such as peer socialization (Raychaudhuri 2018) and social exclusion (Kuo et al. 2016). Asian American identification with the Democratic party may serve as an imperfect proxy for whether they also see themselves as aligned with other racial minorities, who make up the party’s constituency.

But scholars have also argued that minoritized groups like Asian Americans are not as responsive to identity-based threats as previously thought, or may even be demobilized by threat. Using a panel study conducted in the first half of the Trump

The impact of perceived discrimina­ tion on political engagement can also depend on the source of discrimination, where political discrimination (i.e., discrimination that stems from institutions) facilitates participation but societal discrimination (i.e., interpersonal discrimination) can hin­ der it (Oskooii 2016; Oskooii 2020). Our first two hypotheses examine whether perceiving discrimination against Asian Americans will strengthen in-group solidarity, and if it will strengthen Asian Ameri­ can ties to other racial minorities.

Intra-Racial Solidarity (H1): Perceiving discrimination against Asian Ameri­ cans will strengthen feelings of racial solidarity with other Asian Americans.

Inter-Racial Solidarity (H2): Perceiving discrimination against Asian Ameri­ cans will strengthen feelings of racial solidarity with other racially minoritized groups such as Black and Latino Americans.

Perceptions of discrimination are typically operationalized in social science research through survey questions that ask respondents to quantify the amount of discrimina­ tion they perceive. While we, too, rely on such survey measures, they only elucidate one dimension of perception. In the real world context, perceptions of discrimination are not only thought of in terms of quantity or on a linear scale, but they are also imbued with meaning and interpretation in varied ways (Goffman 1974). Strategic actors such as the media and racial group elites play an especially central role in constructing narratives around discrimination and making meaning of group experi­ ences (Kim and Rogers 2021). These narratives shape notions of what the problem is, who or what is causing the problem, and what should be done about it (Benford and Snow 2000). The influence of framing has been tested and found to be significant in a wide variety of political outcomes like policy views, views towards immigrants, and views on events (Berinsky and Kinder 2006; Blinder and Jeannet 2018; Chan, Raychaudhuri, and Valenzuela 2023; Gilens 2009; Raychaudhuri, Mendelberg, and McDonough 2023). Through an original survey experiment, we explore whether bringing forward different considerations around anti-Asian racism than would oth­ erwise be top of mind influences the possibilities for Asian American solidarity.

Methodologically, experimentally examining different frames of anti-Asian rac­ ism in the context of COVID-19 also helps strengthen the external validity of our study. Previous observational studies have studied coalitional attitudes as a product of predispositions such as cross-racial linked fate (Chan and Jasso 2021; Merseth 2018), while experimental studies have used text-based treatments that refer to dis­ crimination in the abstract (Craig and Richeson 2012; Cortland et al. 2017). Our experimental design leverages a historic moment for Asian Amerians and mirrors the informational and psychological environment around anti-Asian racism that Asian Americans have experienced in the last few years.

Study 1: Observational Evidence for Coalitional Attitudes

Do Asian Americans think that there is discrimination against Asian Americans and is this view correlated with coalitional attitudes? We provide initial examinations of these questions using observational data from the 2016 and 2020 Collaborative Multi-Racial Post-Election Survey (CMPS) (Frasure et al. 2021a, 2021b). Using CMPS data, we establish two findings that lay the foundation for our survey experi­ ment. First, Asian American perceptions of anti-Asian racism increased from 2016 to 2020, a distinct trend from perceptions of racism facing other groups. Second, we find that Asian American perceptions of anti-Asian racism is correlated with feelings of solidarity with other minoritized groups.

The 2016 CMPS was fielded in multiple languages, including English, simplified and traditional Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese, and has an oversample of Asian Americans (n = 3,006). The 2020 CMPS was fielded in English, simplified and tra­ ditional Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese, and Urdu, and has an oversample of Asian Americans (n = 5,641). As a result of the oversamples and multiple languages, the CMPS allows us to not only analyze the views of Asian Americans in the aggregate, but also to better understand the views of subgroups of Asian Americans, such as by partisanship and immigrant generation.

As our independent variable, we examine Asian Americans’ perception of anti- Asian discrimination. For both 2016 and 2020, this was measured with a 4-point scale response to the question: “How much discrimination is there against Asian Americans today?”. Responses ranged from “None at all” to “A lot.” This measure captures perceptions of whether Asian Americans as a group are experiencing dis­ crimination, rather than individual experiences. To explore whether perceptions of discrimination against Asian Americans is associated with in-group and out-group allyship, we test the correlation between perceiving anti-Asian discrimination with outcomes including Asian American linked fate, cross-racial linked fate, and views towards the Black Lives Matter movement.

Were Asian Americans Perceiving Greater Discrimination in 2020?

In the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic, Asian Americans were perceiving greater anti-Asian discrimination. From 2016 to 2020, the percent of respondents answering that Asian Americans faced “None at all,” “A little,” or “Some” discrimination all decreased. Meanwhile, the percent of Asian Americans perceiving “A lot” of dis­ crimination against Asian Americans doubled, from 13.2% in 2016 to 27.7% in 2020.

While Asian Americans also perceived slightly more discrimination against Black Americans and Latinx Americans in 2020 compared to 2016 (see Fig. 1 and Appen­ dix Tables A.1-A.4), the increase was not as significant as the change in perceptions

Views Towards Black Lives Matter

We also examined Asian Americans’ attitudes towards the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement. Are Asian Americans who perceive greater discrimination against Asian Americans extending solidarity beyond cross-racial linked fate and actually support­ ing a social movement centered around Black Americans? We looked at whether Asian Americans expressed support for BLM, believed that Asian Americans had a responsibility to support BLM, and felt that Asian Americans would benefit from the success of BLM.4 These measures are from the 2020 CMPS and all categori­ cal responses were recoded to be from 0 to 1 with 1 indicating more support, more responsibility, and more anticipated benefits. We regressed support for, feelings of responsibility towards, and anticipated benefits from BLM on perceiving anti-Asian discrimination while controlling for age, income, female identifying, income, and education. We also controlled for partisanship and immigrant generation except in the subgroup analyses.

Asian Americans who perceived greater anti-Asian discrimination generally expressed more support for, felt more responsibility for, and felt like they would benefit more from BLM (see Fig. 4 and Appendix Table A.8-A.9). These results sug­ gest that Asian Americans have been connecting discrimination against their own group with supporting other racial justice movements. The exception to this finding is Republican Asian Americans, for whom perceiving greater discrimination against Asian Americans is associated with greater support for BLM and belief that they will benefit from the movement, but not higher feelings of responsibility for the success of the movement. Partisanship remains a dividing line in the adoption of coalitional attitudes in a way that immigrant generation is not always, as Asian Americans who perceive more anti-Asian discrimination are more likely to support, feel a respon­ sibility towards, and feel like they will benefit from BLM regardless of immigrant generation.

Study 1 Discussion

Our analyses of the 2016 and 2020 CMPS data establish two important findings. First, Asian Americans are perceiving more anti-Asian discrimination in 2020 compared to 2016. Second, there is fairly consistent evidence showing a correlation between per­ ceptions of anti-Asian racism and feelings of allyship with other minoritized groups.

However, the observational nature of these analyses mean that it can be difficult to piece together a causal mechanism. In other words, we do not know if perceiving anti-Asian discrimination leads to stronger identification with Asian Americans and other racial minorities - only that they are correlated. An alternative explanation for these findings could be that participants who have higher feelings of linked fate are

Our key outcomes tested for attitudinal measures that reflect solidarity within Asian Americans and with other racial minority groups. Respondents were asked to summarize and react to the article, if they read one, in an open-text box. We then asked participants about feelings of closeness and linked fate in relation to Asian Americans, Black Americans, Latino Americans, and White Americans.5 Participants were also asked for their attitudes towards a range of policies, movements, and orga­ nizations from those that are typically considered universal (e.g. Social Security, gov­ ernment-funded healthcare) to ones that are typically associated with a specific racial minority group (e.g. reparations, pathway to citizenship for undocumented immi­ grants, Black Lives Matter, Stop Asian Hate). Additionally, we examined whether respondents felt compelled to take the first step of getting involved by requesting information about various political organizations.

We account for the demographic and political heterogeneity amongst Asian Americans by analyzing immigrant generation subgroups (first generation and second generation and higher) and partisan subsets (Republicans, Democrats, and Independents).6 All difference-in-means tests were conducted relative to the pure control (t0).

Throughout our analyses, we account for multiple hypothesis testing using the “Hommel” method of p-adjustment (Hommel 1988). Figures for Study 2 show 95% confidence intervals but only results which remain statistically significant after adjust­ ing the p-values for multiple hypothesis testing are discussed in the text and shown in black in the figures. All results that are not statistically significant after adjusting the p-values for multiple hypothesis testing are indicated in the figures in gray.

5  Feelings of closeness and linked fate represent two different ways of measuring a sense of collective identity. The former signals perceptions of group proximity, while the latter is theorized as a sense of group solidarity (often derived from shared experiences of discrimination, although not operationalized as such). Both are commonly used in political psychology literature. While linked fate is a canonical concept, scholars have raised concerns about its operationalization (Gay, Hochschild, and White 2016). Thus, using both measures of feelings of closeness and linked fate also provides us with a robustness check.

First, we find that information about anti-Asian discrimination leads Asian Ameri­ cans to express increased feelings of closeness to Latino Americans and Black Amer­ icans. In the full sample, the In-Group Frame increased Asian American feelings of closeness to Black people by 5.5% points (p = 0.004) and to Latinos by 4.3% points (p = 0.014) (see Fig. 5 and Appendix Table E.1). Neither the In-Group Frame nor the Cross-Group Frame led Asian Americans to express more or less feelings of close­ ness with White Americans.

Perhaps surprisingly, the effects are most consistent for Republican Asian Ameri­ cans. When reminded of anti-Asian discrimination via the In-Group Frame, Repub­ lican Asian Americans indicated stronger feelings of closeness to racial minorities across the board. Republican Asian Americans expressed stronger feelings of close­ ness with other Asian Americans by 8.3% points when treated with the In-Group Frame (p = 0.008). Linked Fate

We also find that some respondents’ feelings of linked fate changed when exposed to different frames of anti-Asian racism. In the full sample, the In-Group Frame statisti­ cally significantly increased Asian American feelings of linked fate with Black com­ munities (difference = 0.047, p = 0.034) and Latino communities (difference = 0.023, p = 0.004) (see Fig. 6 and Appendix Table E.2). Similar to feelings of closeness, par­ tisanship remains a divider in how much linked fate is expressed and with whom. For Republican Asian Americans, the In-Group Frame led to higher linked fate with Lati­ nos (difference = 0.153, p = 0). For Democrats, exposure to the In-Group Frame facili­ tated greater linked fate with Black Americans (difference = 0.07, p = 0.016). Neither frame shifted Asian Americans’ feelings of linked fates towards White Americans. In general, for outcomes that explicitly asked Asian Americans to consider their rela­ tionship to other groups such as feelings of closeness and linked fate, the In-Group Frame was more effective in facilitating coalitional attitudes with other racial minori­ ties compared to the Cross-Group Frame. Again, this suggests some evidence for H2 (Interracial Solidarity) but not H3 (Framing).

While we find some evidence for the impact of anti-Asian racism on cross-racial linked fate, we do not find similar effects on intra-racial linked fate (H1). Asian Americans were not moved to greater feelings of intra-Asian American linked fate through various framings of anti-Asian racism, regardless of immigrant generation or partisanship.

We also asked respondents whether they would like to receive information about a variety of intraracial and interracial organization, including both fictional and real groups: the Multi-Racial Coalition to Fight Discrimination, Asian Americans Against Discrimination, Asian Americans Against Affirmative Action, Black Lives Matter, and the Council on American Islamic Relations Campaign to End the Muslim Ban (see Fig. 8 and Appendix Table E.4). We again find some evidence for the importance of how anti-Asian racism is framed, as it is only the Cross-Group Frame that leads respondents to request more information. ## Discussion

In this paper, we focus on Asian Americans to assess the ways in which anti-Asian dis­ crimination influences coalitional attitudes. Using observational data from the 2016 and 2020 CMPS and an original survey experiment, we find that perceptions of anti- Asian racism can facilitate Asian American solidarity with other racial minorities, but it depends on the framing of the issue and which subsets of Asian Americans are in question. Study 1, using observational data from the CMPS, establishes that Asian Americans were perceiving higher levels of anti-Asian racism in 2020 than 2016 and that perceptions of anti-Asian racism were correlated with feelings of linked fate with Asian, Latinx, and Black Americans. Study 2 then explores the impacts of increased salience of anti-Asian racism during the pandemic through a survey experiment. We find that information about anti-Asian racism can shift Asian Americans to express increased feelings of closeness and linked fate with Black and Latino Americans. In particular, Republican Asian Americans, and to a lesser extent, first-generation Asian Americans, are more likely to be moved towards coalitional attitudes than their coun­ terparts who are Democrat or second generation or later. It is the Cross-Group Frame, however, that is more effective at shifting Republican Asian Americans’ policy views on Black Lives Matter, a pathway to citizenship, and reparations.

There are three key takeaways from our results. First, attending to heterogeneity is crucial for understanding Asian American political behavior. We find treatment effects mainly for Republican Asian Americans and first-generation Asian Ameri­ cans. As shown by our analysis of the open-ended text analysis, Republican and firstgeneration Asian Americans were less likely than their Democratic counterparts to express they were already familiar with or unsurprised by issues of anti-Asian rac­ ism. This highlights that information about anti-Asian racism is more impactful on these subgroups who may be less socialized in racial discourses.

Second, we are particularly intrigued by how Republican Asian Americans responded to the Cross-Group Frame. Given that racial justice discourse is concen­ trated in the Democratic party, the Cross-Group Frame should be more challenging for Republican Asian Americans to integrate with their worldviews towards race. Surprisingly, the Cross-Group Frame increased Asian American Republicans’ sup­

port for a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, Black Lives Matter, and reparations for the descendants of enslaved persons - or at least, made Repub­ licans oppose them less. Despite these findings, the Cross-Group treatment did not have much of an impact on Republicans’ sense of linked fate or feelings of close­ ness with other racial minorities. In fact, it was the In-Group Frame that increased Republicans’ feelings of closeness with Asian, Latino, and Black communities at a statistically significant level. While it is promising that Republican Asian Americans were moved in either framing of anti-Asian racism, we are left with the question of why the respective framings impacted different political outcomes. Ultimately, we find change in policy attitudes to be a more tangible result than change in feelings of closeness. This points to the stronger potential of the Cross-Group Frame in facilitat­ ing Asian American solidarity with other racial minorities.

Third, we attribute our mixed findings to a key insight from our analysis of the open-ended text responses: only 43.7% of respondents treated with the Cross-Group Frame mentioned racism facing other racial minorities when asked to summarize the treatment. This indicates to us that after reading the Cross-Group Frame, anti-Asian racism still remained at the forefront of participants’ minds. In contrast, informa­ tion about racism facing other communities of color was not as salient a takeaway for participants. One may attribute this to the treatment design, where the vignette’s discussion of other racial minorities’ experiences was not strong enough to ensure it was a key takeaway for all respondents. However, we argue that our mixed find­ ings and the fact that only a portion of respondents noted racism facing other racial minorities in the open-texted responses is in fact a feature, not a bug. It requires us to contextualize our findings in an analysis of the American racial order and Asian Americans’ place in it. As discussed previously, Asian Americans have been racial­ ized as the most “valorized” racial minority - the model minority, who are lauded for their alleged upward mobility and hard work in the face of racism. These seemingly valorized outcomes are denaturalized when we note the selective immigration poli­ cies that have favored the entry of highly educated Asian immigrants, the ideological function of the model minority to frame racial inequality as a problem of individual responsibility rather than of state responsibility, and the failure to disaggregate the umbrella of “Asian” (Hsu 2015; Junn 2007; Kim 2023; Lee and Zhou 2015; Wu 2013). The racial order is often undertheorized in studies of political behavior, but it is critical in producing a terrain of unequal power and status that shapes individual attitudes and behavior (Carter 2019; Carter, Wong, and Guerrero 2021; Masuoka and Junn 2013). Most relevant for the purpose of this project, the valorization of Asian Americans relative to Black and Latino Americans can undermine Asian Americans’ feelings of solidarity with other communities of color and weaken their ties to each other. Thus for some Asian Americans, even when the increase in anti-Asian hate crimes is placed in the context of the increase in hate crimes against racial minori­ ties more broadly, it may not be enough for them to see shared experiences between themselves and other communities of color.

As the United States rapidly diversifies ethnically, questions remain about whether, when, and how different minoritized groups will work together to advance shared interests (Benjamin 2017; Browning, Marshall, and Tabb 2002; Klein 2020). A strong multiracial coalition could be critical to pushing for greater justice and equity, from

electoral politics that necessitate the building of constituencies to elect candidates and pass legislation, to social movements who seek to organize strong bases of sup­ port across the public and make change (Flexner 1959; McAdam 1982; Olson 1971; Marwell and Oliver 1993; Rosenberg 1991). We offer a hard test of interminority relations with the case of Asian Americans, a group that has often been undertheo­ rized in the intergroup politics literature. We also explore how the political conse­ quences of racial discrimination may be conditional on the framing of the issue.

Our study identifies multiple pathways for future work. First, further work should be done on the contingent nature of Asian American solidarity and how it may be conditional on individual-level political predispositions or demographic identifiers. Interestingly, we saw that Republican and first-generation Asian Americans were most likely to be moved by information about anti-Asian racism. More work should be done to understand how these particular groups develop an understanding of Asian Americans’ relationships to other racial minorities and the extent to which these views are (un)crystallized. Other pre-dispositions and identifiers may also matter. For example, Pérez (2015) showed that xenophobic rhetoric has a stronger impact on the political behavior of Latinos who strongly identify with the group, compared to weak-identifiers. Similarly, we might expect that those who more strongly iden­ tify as Asian Americans are more likely to perceive anti-Asian racism and engage in (inter)group solidarity. Furthermore, while we were unable to fully examine hetero­ geneity by national origin in our survey experiment due to insufficient sample sizes, future research should examine how frames of anti-Asian racism may have differen­ tial mobilizing effects depending on national origin. Previous work has found that different Asian American national origin groups have varying levels of propensity for coalition-building with Black and Latino Americans based on policy preferences (Arora, Sadhwani, and Shah 2021). Possibilities for intergroup solidarity may also depend on the differential effectiveness of identity-based frames for national origin groups considered “prototypical” Asian Americans (e.g. Chinese) compared to those considered “non-prototypical” (Lee and Ramakrishnan 2020).

Second, the power of framing lies in its capacity to provide a common diagnosis of injustices that can then be used as a starting point for different groups to build political alliances. In this study, we tested the impact of framing anti-Asian racism in the context of worsening hate crimes facing communities of color across the board, aiming to build solidarity through pointing to a broader problem that harms multiple communities. Future work should examine what other kinds of frames may encour­ age solidarity. Moreover, framing is only one strategic element of coalitional politics. Coalitional politics also consists of negotiation over tactics, demands, and possibly most crucially, the building of trust and relationships in spite of difference. Scholars should continue to assess what factors matter for the viability and longevity of politi­ cal solidarity, and how that might vary depending on the historical experiences and racial positioning of the groups in question.

Third, our study joins a string of survey experiments about intergroup relations between different racially minoritized groups (Craig and Richeson 2012; Cortland et al. 2017; Pérez et al. 2022). We seek to advance the use of the survey experiment to test the possibilities of cross-racial allyship, by designing our treatments to mirror real-world information environments and assessing how people respond. While we

aim to approximate real-world political behaviors through original outcomes such as seeking information about different organizations, more work is left to be done on how to close the gap between experimental settings and the realities of solidarity on the ground.

Questions around Asian Americans’ relationships to other communities of color are especially central given how Asian Americans are positioned in the racial order as a valorized racial minority. Anti-Asian racism fueled by the racialization of COVID- 19 has the potential to be a definitive moment for Asian American communities. On one hand, this moment has brought race-based considerations to the forefront for Asian American engagement in politics (Chan, Nguy, and Masuoka 2022). Hundreds of Asian American organizations across the country signed on to an open letter spear­ headed by Asian Americans Advancing Justice Atlanta, after the murder of 8 people, 6 of whom were Korean and Chinese women, at spas and massage parlors in Atlanta, calling for community-based solutions to violence. This letter explicitly positioned Asians as aligned with other communities of color, stating: “Violence against Asian American communities is part of a larger system of violence and racism against all communities of color, including Black, Brown, and Indigenous communities” (Asian Americans Advancing Justice - Atlanta and Georgia NAACP 2021).

At the same time, at the local and state levels, Asian Americans have shifted to the right. In 2021, Asian Americans, primarily Chinese Americans, played a crucial role in the recall of San Francisco’s progressive District Attorney Chesa Boudin. In the 2022 governor’s race in New York, Democratic margins decreased in majority- Asian precincts in New York City compared to 2018, with some precincts flipping to Republican majorities (Leonhardt 2023). In both of these cases, concerns over crime and safety in light of anti-Asian racism have propelled Asian Americans to the right. Disinformation has also been prevalent around COVID-related anti-Asian racism, reinvigorating the trope of Black-Asian conflict as the media sensationalized cases where perpetrators of anti-Asian incidents were Black (Asian American Disinforma­ tion Table 2022). The narrative around anti-Asian racism has shifted from fighting against white supremacist rhetoric to being fixated on cases involving an alleged Black suspect, when studies have shown that most cases of anti-Asian racism are per­ petuated by white individuals (Wong and Liu 2022). We anticipate that for some of our respondents, this misperception that Black Americans are the primary perpetra­ tors of anti-Asian racism counteracts narratives that seek to connect Asian Americans and other communities of color, forming a barrier to Asian American engagement in solidarity politics.

All these trends, along with our findings, reveal that we should not take for granted that the heightened discussion about anti-Asian racism is sufficient to shift Asian American attitudes towards solidarity with other communities of color. Rather, anti- Asian racism can be framed and mobilized in a variety of ways that shape its political consequences. The work, after all, of social movements is to delineate and convey who is affected by an issue and what should be done about it (Benford and Snow 2000). The issue of anti-Asian racism has already become a driving force for Asian American politics, whether towards the left or the right, and we show that it is par­ ticularly consequential for the political behavior of Republican and first-generation Asian Americans. While Asian Americans have become a fairly consistent Demo­
